title: How Many Different Island Shapes
statement:
`grid` is a map of `1` (land) and `0` (water). An **island** is a group of land cells connected through their sides (up, down, left, right). Two islands have the **same shape** if one can be moved onto the other **by sliding it** (translation) without rotating or flipping it.

Return the number of **different island shapes**.

examples.explanation: An L-shaped island of three cells and a vertical pair of cells: two different shapes.
Four single-cell islands all have the same shape.

hints.nudge: Two islands that are translations of each other have the same cells relative to their top-left corner. How could you write an island down so that equal shapes give equal descriptions?
hints.pattern: Find every island with a flood fill; describe it by the positions of its cells relative to its first cell (or by the path of the search); put the descriptions into a set; the answer is the size of the set.
hints.pseudocode:
shapes = empty set
for each unvisited land cell (r0, c0): collect the cells of its island with a flood fill
  shape = sorted list of (r - r0, c - c0) for every cell, where (r0, c0) is the first cell found in row-major order
  add shape to shapes
return the size of shapes
hints.walkthrough: Sliding an island does not change the offsets of its cells from a fixed reference cell. Scanning the grid row by row, the first land cell of an island you meet is its top-most (and, in that row, left-most) cell, which is the same part of the shape wherever the island lies. So record each cell as (row - row0, column - column0) relative to that cell. Sort the offsets (or collect them in the same order), turn the list into something you can store in a set (a tuple or a text), and add it. Rotated or mirrored copies produce different offset lists, which is exactly what the problem wants. Another way is to record the sequence of moves of the depth-first search, including a mark when it backtracks. O(rows * columns).
